summary.title: Death By a Thousand Microservices
summary.one_liner: Microservices add heavy operational complexity (tooling, testing, duplicated plumbing, ownership friction) that most companies don't need, and a well-run monolith or a few "branch" services is often the better choice.
takeaways: Microservices bring costs in development, debugging, deployment, testing and resilience that are often underestimated.
Per-service boilerplate, duplicated code and per-service CI/CD setup make developer ergonomics worse as the number of services grows.
Integration testing a distributed system is hard, and observability becomes an expensive substitute for it.
Many large products (e.g. Shopify, Stack Overflow, WhatsApp) began or remain as monoliths, so a monolith is not inherently a mistake.
A practical alternative is to start with a monolith and extract separately scalable 'branch' services only when a clear load or scaling need exists.
summary.summary: The author, a long-time engineer, argues that the industry adopted microservices by default, driven by hype, venture-funded hiring, and copied big-tech practices, rather than by real scale needs. The essay lists specific pitfalls: loss of DRY code, poor developer ergonomics, weak integration testing, and team ownership friction across services. It cites examples of successful monolithic companies and small teams, and suggests starting with a monolith or a "trunk and branches" design where only clearly scalable workloads are split out. The tone is opinionated and polemical, with few hard measurements and mostly anecdotal evidence.
